603.title: Fields white for harvest (John 4:27–42)
603.hook: she leaves her water jar and tells the town; many believe
603.howItsDone: Some Christians turn to this passage when they talk about sharing their faith, hearing in the woman's "come, see" a model of inviting someone rather than arguing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Samaritan woman at the well at noon, and a conversation that crossed an old divide. Your line was in spirit and in truth. Where did you find God without a building? Day six hundred three.

Just as Jesus tells her who he is, the disciples come back with lunch. John says they marveled that he was talking with a woman, and nobody dared ask him why. A group of men holding bread, standing awkwardly. And the woman doesn't wait for anyone to explain. She turns and walks fast back toward town. And she leaves something behind, sitting by the well. The one thing she came for. The text says it in one quiet line: "The woman then left her waterpot, and went her way into the city."

Why mention the jar? It was the whole reason for her trip. Leaving it says she's in a hurry, and maybe that she'll be back. Some readers also hear something more: she came for ordinary water and found what Jesus called living water, so the old jar can wait. In town, her message is simple, almost funny: "Come, see a man, which told me all things that ever I did: is not this the Christ?" Not a sermon. An invitation, and a question. Come and see, close to the words Philip used with Nathanael back in chapter one. Meanwhile, back at the well, the disciples are pushing food at Jesus. Master, eat. And he says, "I have meat to eat that ye know not of." Meat, in the King James English, just means food. They wonder if someone brought him something to eat. He explains: his food is to do the will of the one who sent him. Then he points at the fields. "Say not ye, There are yet four months, and then cometh harvest? behold, I say unto you, Lift up your eyes, and look on the fields; for they are white already to harvest." Some readers picture the townspeople at that very moment, streaming out across the fields toward the well, maybe in light-colored clothes. The text doesn't say so, but the timing fits. And the ending: many of the Samaritans, John says, believe because of her word. Then Jesus stays two days, and more believe, and they tell her: "Now we believe, not because of thy saying: for we have heard him ourselves." She brought them; they met him themselves. And they call him the Savior of the world.

Here's the practice: leave something behind in your hurry to share. Settle, and breathe. Think of something good that happened to you lately. A kindness, a book, a moment that opened something. Who would want to hear about it? Picture their face. Then think of your water jar: the small thing that usually stops you sharing. Being busy. Worrying it'll sound strange. Let it sit by the well for a minute. If you pray, you can ask for the nerve to say come and see. If you don't, just rest with the person you pictured. The bell holds the time.
Fields white for harvest. Jesus's words as the Samaritan town comes out to meet him: the harvest isn't months away, it's already here.
Your line: she left her water jar. Today, tell one person about something good, and let one small task wait while you do. Day six hundred three.

604.title: Go, your son lives (John 4:43–54)
604.hook: a royal official believes the word and walks home
604.tomorrow: do you want to be healed?
604.howItsDone: Some Christians turn to this story when someone they love is ill and far away, and some churches pray for the sick by name during worship.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the woman ran back to town and the Samaritans came out across the fields. Your line was she left her water jar. Who did you tell, and what did you let wait? Day six hundred four.

A man with rank, and none of it helps. The King James calls him a nobleman, an official of the king, and his son is sick, at the point of death, in Capernaum. He hears Jesus is back in Galilee, at Cana, the village of the wedding. He goes up to find him. Every hour he's gone is an hour he's not at his son's bed. He finds Jesus, and he doesn't make a speech. He begs: "Sir, come down ere my child die." Come down. Come with me. Now.

Jesus's first answer sounds like a sigh, aimed at the whole crowd as much as at him: "Except ye see signs and wonders, ye will not believe." The father doesn't argue. He just asks again. Come down before my child dies. And Jesus doesn't come. He says one short sentence, which the King James Bible gives as: "Go thy way; thy son liveth." That's all. No touch, no visit, no proof. Just a sentence, and a long road. Then John writes the line that is today's carry: "And the man believed the word that Jesus had spoken unto him, and he went his way." Think about that walk. He's begged for Jesus to come, and he's leaving without him, carrying nothing but a sentence. The next day, still on the road, his servants come running to meet him. Your son lives. He asks them one question: when did he start getting better? They tell him: "Yesterday at the seventh hour the fever left him." The very hour Jesus said go. And John says the man believed, and his whole household with him. Notice that the word believe appears twice. First he believes the word, enough to start walking. Then, when he sees what happened, he believes in a fuller way. Here faith grows in two steps: first a step on trust, then sight. John counts this as the second sign Jesus did in Galilee, after the water turned to wine, and both happen from Cana. One at a wedding, one by a word spoken from a distance.
screen: `A LONG ROAD WITH ONLY A SENTENCE.`
then, large: `THE MAN BELIEVED THE WORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take a word on trust. Settle, and breathe. Think of a promise or a word someone has given you that you can't check yet. A friend who said I'll be there. A doctor who said this will heal. A line from scripture you hold onto. Notice whether some part of you wants proof first. Then imagine taking the first step home anyway, the way the father did, with only the sentence in your pocket. If you pray, you can hold that word before God. If you don't, rest with that word a moment. The bell holds the time.
Go. Jesus's answer to a desperate father: go thy way, thy son liveth. One word that sends him home on nothing but trust.
Your line: he believed the word. Today, act on one thing someone told you in good faith, without asking for proof first. Day six hundred four.

605.title: Do you want to be healed? (John 5:1–9)
605.word: Do you want to be healed?
605.hook: a man by the pool thirty-eight years; Jesus asks the obvious question
605.carry: do you want to be well?
605.howItsDone: Christians often read this story in services of prayer for healing; some churches anoint the sick with oil, and many simply pray for people by name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a royal official walked twenty miles home with nothing but a sentence: go, thy son liveth. Your line was he believed the word. What did you take on trust? Day six hundred five.

Jerusalem, near the Sheep Gate. A pool surrounded by covered walkways, and under them, crowds of sick people lying on mats: blind, lame, withered. John names the place: "Now there is at Jerusalem by the sheep market a pool, which is called in the Hebrew tongue Bethesda, having five porches." For centuries some readers thought the five porches were invented, a symbol. Then archaeologists dug near the Church of Saint Anne in Jerusalem and found two large pools with colonnades: four around the sides and one across the middle. Five. Under one of those porches lies a man who has been ill for thirty-eight years.

Jesus sees him, learns how long he's been there, and asks a question that sounds almost rude: "Wilt thou be made whole?" Do you want to be well? Of course he does. Doesn't he? But listen to his answer. He doesn't say yes. "Sir, I have no man, when the water is troubled, to put me into the pool: but while I am coming, another steppeth down before me." People believed the first one into the pool when the water stirred would be healed. And this man has no one. Thirty-eight years, and not one friend to carry him the last few feet. His answer is a list of reasons, and underneath it, loneliness. That's why the question isn't rude. After a long time, a life gets built around what's wrong. Your days, your friends, even your sense of who you are. Being well would change everything, and change is frightening. Jesus doesn't argue, and he doesn't use the pool. He says, "Rise, take up thy bed, and walk." And the text: "And immediately the man was made whole, and took up his bed, and walked: and on the same day was the sabbath." That last phrase is a fuse, and it goes off tomorrow. One more detail for the curious. Some older Bibles, including the King James, have a verse about an angel stirring the water. The earliest Greek manuscripts don't include it, so many modern Bibles put it in a footnote. Either way, John's story doesn't turn on the pool. It turns on the question.
screen: then, large: `DO YOU WANT TO BE WELL?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: answer the question honestly for yourself. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing in your life that isn't well. A habit, a hurt, a grudge, a pattern you keep repeating. Now hear the question: do you want to be well? Don't answer quickly. Notice if your first answer is a reason, like the man's. I have no one. It's too late. Someone always gets there first. Then ask what might change if it got better, and whether part of you is afraid of that. If you pray, you can bring the honest answer to God. If you don't, simply hold it gently. The bell holds the time.
Do you want to be healed? Jesus's question to a man ill for thirty-eight years, who answered with reasons and then got up and walked.
screen: `DO YOU WANT TO BE HEALED? — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: do you want to be well? Today, take one small step toward the thing you named, even if all you do is tell someone about it. Day six hundred five.

606.title: My Father works (John 5:10–30)
606.hook: healing on the sabbath: my Father is working still, and so am I
606.howItsDone: Christians read this passage as a teaching about Jesus as the Son of God; some also see in it a call to join in God's ongoing work of healing and care.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a man thirty-eight years by the pool, and a question that wasn't as obvious as it sounded. Your line was do you want to be well? What step did you take? Day six hundred six.

The healed man is walking through Jerusalem with his rolled-up mat under his arm. It's the sabbath, the day of rest that Jewish law protects. Some of the religious leaders stop him: it is not lawful, they say, to carry your bed today. And his answer is wonderfully human: the man who healed me told me to. Who was it? He doesn't know. He never got the name. Jesus had slipped away into the crowd. Later Jesus finds him in the temple. And now the question of the sabbath reaches Jesus himself.

When Jesus finds the man in the temple, he tells him: "Behold, thou art made whole: sin no more, lest a worse thing come unto thee." The man goes and tells the leaders who healed him. And the argument begins. Remember, this is a debate among Jews, about what keeping the sabbath means. Jesus's answer is a single sentence: "My Father worketh hitherto, and I work." Hitherto means until now. My Father is still working, so I am too. Genesis says God rested on the seventh day. Yet the world keeps going on the sabbath. Babies are born, rain falls, hearts beat. Jewish teachers asked the same question: how can God rest, when the world needs holding up every moment? Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish writer of that time, answered that God never stops making and sustaining the world. Jesus takes that thought and stands inside it. If the Father is still at work, the Son works with him. His listeners hear the claim clearly: he is calling God his own Father, making himself equal with God. Then Jesus describes how it works between them: "The Son can do nothing of himself, but what he seeth the Father do." Like an apprentice at a workbench, watching the master's hands and copying them. In Christian teaching, this passage is a key to who Jesus is: not a rival to God, but the Son doing what the Father does. And in Jesus's words it's also a picture of a God who doesn't clock out, still at the work of healing and giving life.
screen: then, large: `MY FATHER WORKETH HITHERTO, AND I WORK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one good work today. Settle, and breathe. Notice what is working in you right now without any effort. Your heart beating. Your lungs filling. The ground holding you up. Then think of one good piece of work you could do today. Something that heals or helps, even a small thing: a message to someone lonely, a repair you've put off, carrying something for someone. Picture yourself doing it. If you pray, you can ask to see where God is already at work, and join in. If you don't, choose the work anyway. The bell holds the time.
My Father works. Jesus's answer when he healed on the sabbath: God is still at work, and the Son works with him.
Your line: god is still working. Today, do the one good work you chose, and look for one sign that healing is still going on around you. Day six hundred six.

607.title: Search the scriptures (John 5:31–47)
607.hook: you search the scriptures, yet won't come to me
607.howItsDone: Some Christians read a Bible passage every day, and some practice slow, prayerful reading such as lectio divina, listening for God speaking through the text rather than only studying it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a healed man carried his mat on the sabbath, and Jesus said my Father worketh hitherto. Your line was god is still working. What good work did you do? Day six hundred seven.

You can know everything about a person and still not know them. You can read every review of a restaurant and never eat there. You can study a map of a city for years and never walk its streets. Jesus is still in the middle of yesterday's argument in Jerusalem, and now it turns to evidence. Who says you are who you say you are? In that world, a claim needed witnesses. The law of Moses said a matter stands on two or three. So Jesus calls his witnesses, one by one, the way a lawyer would. The last one is a book.

First witness: John the Baptist. Jesus says of him, "He was a burning and a shining light." People were glad to stand in that light for a while. Second witness: the works. The healings, the signs, the man walking with his mat. Third: the Father himself. And fourth: the scriptures. Here's the famous line, in the King James Bible: "Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me." There's a puzzle hiding in the Greek. The verb can be read two ways. It can be a command, search the scriptures, which is how the King James translators took it. Or it can be a plain statement: you search the scriptures. Other translations read it that way. Same Greek letters, both readings possible. Either way, the next line is the point: "And ye will not come to me, that ye might have life." Jesus doesn't tell them to stop searching. They search, he says, because they think eternal life is in those pages. His point is about where reading leads. A map points to a city. A letter points to the one who wrote it. In Christian reading, the scriptures are meant to lead to a living person, not just to more knowledge about him. Christians read this line in different ways. Some hear it about the Old Testament promises that Christians see fulfilled in Jesus. Others hear a warning for anyone who studies: it's possible to know the text by heart and miss the one it's about.
screen: then, large: `THEY ARE THEY WHICH TESTIFY OF ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read to meet someone, not just to know. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a short passage you know: a psalm, a line from the Gospels, or a few words from this path so far. Say it slowly in your head. Then, instead of asking what it means, ask who is speaking, and what they might be like. Listen for a person behind the words. If you pray, you can ask to meet the one the words are about. If you don't, simply notice the difference between reading for facts and listening for a voice. The bell holds the time.
Search the scriptures. Jesus's words about the writings that testify of him: reading meant to lead to a person, not only to knowledge.
Your line: the scriptures point to him. Today, read one verse, and ask not what it says, but who it shows you. Day six hundred seven.

608.title: Twelve baskets left (John 6:1–15)
608.hook: gather the fragments so nothing is lost
608.howItsDone: Some Christians give thanks before meals, as Jesus does here, and some churches run food banks and community meals, gathering surplus food so nothing is wasted.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jesus called his witnesses, and the last was a book. Your line was the scriptures point to him. Which verse did you read, and who did it show you? Day six hundred eight.

A crowd on a grassy hillside by the Sea of Galilee, about five thousand men, John says. And John notes that Passover is near, the feast that remembers the night Israel left Egypt. Jesus looks at the crowd and asks Philip a question, as a test: where shall we buy bread for all these? Philip does the math and gives up: "Two hundred pennyworth of bread is not sufficient for them, that every one of them may take a little." Not even a little each. Then Andrew notices a boy.

Andrew says: "There is a lad here, which hath five barley loaves, and two small fishes: but what are they among so many?" Matthew, Mark and Luke tell this story too, but John is the one who mentions the boy, and that the loaves were barley. A kid's lunch, offered to a crowd. Jesus has everyone sit down on the grass. He takes the loaves, gives thanks, and hands them out, and the fish too, as much as anyone wants. Everyone eats until they're full. The Gospels don't describe how it happened. They only describe what people saw: enough. Then comes the part this day is named for. Jesus says to the disciples: "Gather up the fragments that remain, that nothing be lost." They go around the hillside collecting broken pieces, and they fill twelve baskets. Think about that instruction. A miracle has just happened, and the next thing Jesus cares about is the crumbs. Nothing wasted. Nothing thrown away. Twelve baskets, one for each disciple doing the gathering, maybe, or a number some readers connect with the twelve tribes of Israel. All four Gospels tell this feeding, and some Christians hear in it a picture of the Lord's Supper too: he took bread, gave thanks, and gave it. And the scene ends strangely. The crowd is so excited they want to seize Jesus and make him king by force. And he slips away alone, up the mountain. He came to feed them, not to be crowned by them.

Here's the practice: use up leftovers. Settle, and breathe. Picture your kitchen. What's sitting in the fridge or the cupboard that might get thrown out? Half a loaf, a few vegetables, last night's rice. Make a plan to use one thing today. Then widen it. What else in your life is a fragment you've stopped noticing? A half-finished letter. An hour you usually waste. A small skill nobody asks for. If you pray, you can give thanks for what's already there, the way Jesus gave thanks over a boy's lunch. If you don't, simply notice how much is there. The bell holds the time.
Twelve baskets left. After five thousand ate, the disciples gathered the fragments, so that nothing would be lost.
Your line: let nothing be lost. Today, cook or eat one leftover instead of throwing it out, and notice one other thing worth saving. Day six hundred eight.

609.title: It is I (John 6:16–21)
609.hook: rowing in the dark, they see him and he says: it is I, be not afraid
609.tomorrow: I am the bread of life
609.howItsDone: Some Christians turn to this story in times of fear, and "be not afraid" is repeated in prayers, in hymns and at bedsides.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a boy's five barley loaves fed a hillside, and the disciples gathered twelve baskets of fragments. Your line was let nothing be lost. What did you save from the trash? Day six hundred nine.

Evening. Jesus is still alone up the mountain, and the disciples don't wait. They go down to the shore, get into the boat, and start rowing across the lake toward Capernaum. John gives it one line: "And it was now dark, and Jesus was not come to them." Then a great wind blows, and the sea rises. They row, and row. Far out on the lake, in the dark, they see something on the water.

"So when they had rowed about five and twenty or thirty furlongs, they see Jesus walking on the sea, and drawing nigh unto the ship: and they were afraid." And here is what he says: "It is I; be not afraid." In English, it is I sounds like any friend calling out in the dark. It's me. But in Greek, the words are ego eimi, which simply means I am. It's the ordinary way to say it's me. Some readers also hear in it the name God gives Moses at the burning bush, I AM. John will use those two words again, and some readers hear both meanings here at once: it's me, your friend, and I AM, out on the water, where in the book of Job it is God who treads upon the waves. Then the comfort: be not afraid. Fear not is said often in the Bible. Angels say it. Prophets say it. Jesus says it more than once. And John's ending is lovely and strange: "Then they willingly received him into the ship: and immediately the ship was at the land whither they went." No calming of the storm is described. Just him in the boat, and suddenly the shore. Look back over this week: a water jar left at a well, a father walking home on a word, a man asked if he wanted to be well, God still working, the scriptures pointing, twelve baskets, and now a voice in the dark.
screen: `HE GETS IN, AND THERE'S THE SHORE.`
then, large: `IT IS I; BE NOT AFRAID.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one fear in the dark. Settle, and breathe. Close your eyes if you like, so it's a little dark. Let one fear come up that you've been rowing against. Money, health, someone you love, something you said. Don't fight it. Just name it, quietly, in a few words. Then imagine hearing a voice across the water, one you trust: be not afraid. Notice what happens in your body when you hear it. If you pray, you can invite Jesus into the boat with that fear. If you don't, let the words be a kindness to yourself. The bell holds the time.
It is I. In Greek, ego eimi: it's me, and also I am. What Jesus says to his friends in the dark, on the water.
Your line: be not afraid. Today, when the fear you named shows up, say the line to yourself once, and keep rowing. Day six hundred nine, and another week on the path.
